summary: The Tank 300 Hi4-T is the plug-in version of GWM's boxy body-on-frame off-roader, and Australian reviewers agree it is the cheapest way into a genuinely capable plug-in 4x4 — a 37.11kWh battery, a mechanical transfer case with front and rear locking diffs, and a 3000kg braked tow rating for about $56,000, where the only other plug-in SUV rated to tow 3000kg here costs more than twice as much. They also agree on where it falls down: the drivetrain calibration is the most-criticised thing about the car, with CarsGuide calling the throttle response 'awful' and carsales and EV Central both describing hesitation between petrol and electric power. Scores land in a narrow band — Chasing Cars 8.0/10, carsales 76/100 — and every reviewer makes the same caveat, that the running-cost case rests entirely on charging at home, because once the battery is flat this is a 2.6-tonne petrol 4x4 drinking 10 to 12L/100km.
pros: A 3000kg braked tow rating with a genuine mechanical transfer case and front and rear locking differentials, at $55,990 — the only other plug-in hybrid SUV on sale in Australia rated to 3000kg is the Land Rover Defender 110 P300e, which starts at over $131,000, and every cheaper plug-in SUV tops out at 1500-2500kg

The 37.11kWh pack is the largest in any plug-in hybrid SUV under $60,000 here, claiming 115km of electric range, and independent testers got closer to the claim than usual: Chasing Cars saw 85-95km and EV Central about 90km, enough to cover a typical commute on the plug alone

300kW and 750Nm for a claimed 6.3sec 0-100km/h, plus 50kW DC fast charging on CCS2 (30-80 per cent in about 24 minutes) and 6kW vehicle-to-load — DC charging is rare at this price and lets the pack be usefully topped up on a trip rather than only overnight
7-year/unlimited-km unconditional warranty with no dealer-servicing condition attached, plus separate 8-year/unlimited-km cover on the drive battery

Undercuts the Denza B5, its nearest plug-in off-road rival, by roughly $19,000 ($74,990), which is why reviewers repeatedly describe it as the cheapest serious plug-in hybrid four-wheel drive on sale in Australia
cons: The 1.9L/100km label figure is meaningless once the battery is flat: GWM's own low-charge figure is 8.3L/100km, and testers did worse again — CarsGuide recorded 11.0L/100km around town and 8.5L/100km in the country, Chasing Cars about 10L/100km in town, and EV Central over 12L/100km on the freeway. A buyer who cannot charge at home is running a 2.6-tonne petrol four-wheel drive

Electric range is quoted on the superseded NEDC cycle only and no WLTP figure exists for this car — GWM does not sell the Tank 300 in the UK or continental Europe, so the Hi4-T has never been type-approved there and there is no European number to fall back on. Read 115km as an optimistic upper bound against the 85-95km testers actually returned

Practicality is thin for a 4.76m off-roader: 360L behind the second row (1520L folded) is less than the coupe-rooflined Haval H6 GT PHEV manages, payload is only 610kg, and the 3000kg tow rating sits 500kg below GWM's own Cannon Alpha PHEV ute and a diesel Ford Everest or Toyota Prado

Drivability is the consistent complaint across every Australian review: CarsGuide calls the throttle calibration 'awful' with a hesitant initial response followed by a surge, carsales notes laggy powertrain response and a jittery ride, EV Central describes hesitation handing over between power sources, and Chasing Cars reports cabin creaks and a lumpy on-road ride. The part-time four-wheel-drive system also cannot be used on sealed roads

Pricing is campaign-driven rather than stable — GWM launched both grades at $55,990 and $59,990 drive-away and then added $2,000 on 1 June 2026, taking the drive-away figures to $57,990 and $61,990 — and the Chinese-market Tank 300L facelift with a 59.6kWh pack and roughly double the electric range is already public, which would date this car sharply if it reaches Australia
